content: A sneeze, also known as the photic sneeze reflex or Peroutka sneeze, is a semi-autonomous, convulsive expulsion of air from the lungs. Sneezing occurs when particles bypass the nasal hairs and reach the nasal mucosa, triggering the release of histamines. These histamines stimulate nerve cells in the nose, which then send a signal to the brain to initiate the sneeze reflex. The brain responds by creating a large opening in the nasal cavity to facilitate the expulsion of irritants. In some individuals, exposure to bright light can also trigger sneezing, a phenomenon referred to as the photic sneeze reflex. Suppressing or holding back a sneeze can lead to damage in the sinuses and inner ear due to the backflow of air pressure. This can result in symptoms such as tinnitus, reduced high-frequency hearing, or, in severe cases, a ruptured eardrum. A single sneeze can produce approximately 40,000 droplets, each measuring 5 to 5 micrometers in diameter. Historically, sneezing has been associated with divine or symbolic significance. In 410 BC, the Athenian general Xenophon delivered a motivational speech to his soldiers, urging them to fight for liberty against the Persians. At the conclusion of his speech, a soldier sneezed, which was interpreted as a favorable sign from the gods. This bolstered the soldiers' morale, and they followed Xenophon’s command. Similarly, in Greek mythology, sneezing is mentioned in the story of Odysseus. When Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, spoke to his wife Penelope about his return, their son sneezed loudly. Penelope interpreted this as a divine sign, reassuring her of Odysseus’s safe return. In various cultures, sneezing without an apparent cause is believed to indicate that someone is talking about the person who sneezed. This belief is particularly prevalent in Japanese culture. The sound of a sneeze is often represented through onomatopoeia in different languages. In English, common representations include achoo, achew, or atisshoo, with the first syllable mimicking the intake of air and the second representing the sneeze itself. In Cypriot Greek, the sound is apshoo, which is also the name of a village. In French, the sound is atchoum, and in Japanese, it is hakushou. Cultural responses to sneezing vary widely. In English-speaking countries, it is customary to say God bless you or simply Bless you after someone sneezes. This tradition dates back to the Middle Ages when it was believed that sneezing caused the heart to stop and the soul to momentarily leave the body, making it vulnerable to evil spirits. Saying God bless you was thought to protect the sneezer. Today, this phrase is used as a polite gesture, often followed by the sneezer saying Thank you. During the outbreak of scarlet fever, the phrase God bless you was also used in the hope of survival. In other cultures, phrases referencing health or well-being are commonly used. For example, Germans say Gesundheit, which means health. In Spanish, the phrase Salud is used, meaning to your health. Similarly, in Finnish, the word terveydeksi is used, and in Romanian, people say Sănătate (health) or Noroc (luck). In Hebrew, the phrase לבריאות (labri’ut) means to health. In Scandinavian countries, the word prosit, derived from Latin, means may it benefit you. In Russian, the phrase будь здоров(а/ы) (bud’ zdorov/a/y) translates to be healthy. In Armenian, people say առողջություն (aroghjootyoon), meaning health. In Turkish, the phrase Çok yaşa means live long, to which the response is Sen de gör, meaning may you see it too. In Arabic, particularly in the Jordanian dialect, people say صحة (Sahha), meaning health, or نشوة (Nashweh), meaning ecstasy. The response is often شكراً (Shukran, thank you) or تسلم (Taslam, may you be kept safe). In French, after the first sneeze, one says à tes souhaits. meaning to your wishes. If the same person sneezes again, the response is à tes amours. meaning to your loves. Among Muslims, the practice of responding to sneezes is rooted in Prophetic traditions. According to Al-Bukhari (6224), the Prophet Muhammad instructed that when someone sneezes, they should say Al-hamdu-Lillah (Praise be to Allah), and their companion should respond accordingly. In Dutch, people commonly say gezondheid (health) or proost (cheers) after a sneeze.
